blocks.text: The term species is a fundamental concept in biology. A species is generally defined as a group of individuals that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring under natural conditions. Members of the same species share common characteristics and genetic make-up, which distinguishes them from the individuals of other species.

Identifying species by physical traits and similarities can sometimes be a problem because of cryptic species: organisms that look alike but are genetically distinct. To address this, the German-American biologist Ernst Mayr emphasised reproductive isolation as the key criterion. According to this concept, species are groups of interbreeding natural populations. Members of different species do not normally mate with each other or produce viable, fertile offspring.

blocks.title: Biological species concept
blocks.text: A species is a group of interbreeding natural populations that is reproductively isolated from other such groups. The test is not how organisms look but whether they breed together and produce fertile offspring.

blocks.title: Why appearance is not enough
blocks.text: Cryptic species look the same but are genetically distinct and do not interbreed. The reverse also happens: individuals of one species can look very different, as dog breeds do, yet still belong to one species because they interbreed and produce fertile young.

Speciation is the evolutionary process by which new species arise from a common ancestor. It involves the accumulation of genetic changes that lead to reproductive isolation between populations. There are several mechanisms of speciation.

Allopatric speciation occurs when a population is geographically separated into two or more isolated groups. The groups experience different environments and evolve independently. Over time the accumulated differences can become large enough to prevent interbreeding, even if the geographical barrier is later removed. An example is the speciation of Darwin's finches on the Galapagos Islands, where different populations adapted to diverse environments.

Peripatric speciation involves a small, isolated population at the edge of a larger population. The small population undergoes rapid evolutionary change and diverges from the original population. An example is seen in island species that evolve from a small founding population.

Parapatric speciation occurs when populations are adjacent to each other but occupy different environments along a gradient. Gene flow between the populations is limited, and each evolves adaptations to its own environment; over time this can lead to reproductive isolation. An example is the grass Anthoxanthum odoratum, which shows different adaptations to varying soil conditions across a gradient, leading to reproductive isolation between plants on different soils.

In sympatric speciation new species arise within the same geographical area, without physical barriers. It often happens through polyploidy, in which an organism has multiple sets of chromosomes, or through niche differentiation, in which different subpopulations exploit different resources. For instance, certain plants undergo polyploidy, which leads to immediate reproductive isolation and the formation of new species.

blocks.alt: Four columns, one per mode of speciation, each read downward through the same rows: original population, initial step, reproductive isolation, speciation. Allopatric: a geographical barrier splits the population. Peripatric: a small edge group moves into an isolated niche. Parapatric: a group enters an adjacent niche with limited gene flow. Sympatric: a subgroup takes up a new niche in the same area.
blocks.caption: The four modes of speciation (original diagram after Figure 1.32).
blocks.long_description: Every mode starts with one population and ends with two species, but the initial step differs: a geographical barrier (allopatric), a small group isolated at the edge (peripatric), a neighbouring niche along a gradient (parapatric), or a new niche inside the same area (sympatric). In each case reproductive isolation comes before speciation.

items: A species is a group of individuals that interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring; Ernst Mayr made reproductive isolation the key test.
Cryptic species look alike but are genetically distinct, which is why appearance alone can mislead.
Speciation is the origin of new species from a common ancestor through genetic changes that cause reproductive isolation.
Allopatric: geographical barrier. Peripatric: small edge population. Parapatric: adjacent environments along a gradient. Sympatric: same area, through polyploidy or niche differentiation.

blocks.prompt: Two populations of a plant grow side by side on acidic and alkaline soil and no longer interbreed. Which mode of speciation is this, and how does it differ from sympatric speciation?
blocks.explanation: Parapatric speciation: the populations are adjacent along a soil gradient with limited gene flow, as in Anthoxanthum odoratum. Sympatric speciation happens within one shared area with no spatial separation at all, for example through polyploidy.
